Pete. Bakery's got nothing going at the minute. Alan's cut the shifts back since Christmas, not taking on. Covering the odd day, maybe, if Gary's off sick, but I wouldn't count on it. Have you tried the Corner Stores? Dave's mate Sanjay's always short on staff.
Right. Sanjay at the Corner Stores — do you know if he's after anyone full-time or just weekends? And what's he paying? I need to know what I'm working with.

Right, Pete. Sanjay's mostly after weekends, from what Dave says. Full-time, I wouldn't bet on it. Pay's not much above minimum as far as I know, so ring him before you plan around it. Don't say I sent you, mind. He's a hard man to get a yes out of.

act.text: Ring Sanjay at Corner Stores re weekend work, pay rate. Ask Dave for contact. Also ask Lewis about jobs.

transcript: Lewis, Pete Bevan. Have you got any work at the Food Hall — shelf-stacking, deliveries, garden bits out the back? I need something regular.

Pete. Work's thin, I won't dress it up. I've got Owen on the shop floor and takings barely cover wages some weeks. What I could use is someone for deliveries and the bits out the back — a few hours, not full-time money. What sort of regular are you after, and what can you do?

A few hours is a start, but I'll be straight with you — I need it to add up. What's the rate, and how many hours a week are we talking? If it's steady, even part-time, I'll take it and keep looking for the rest. I can do deliveries, lifting, and I'm handy in a garden — the back of the Food Hall could do with a tidy-up, I'd wager.

Straight answer then: I can give you eight hours a week, deliveries and the back yard, at twelve dollars an hour — that's ninety-six a week, paid on the Friday like the rest of us. It's not full-time money and I won't pretend it is. If that works for you, start Wednesday morning and we'll see how the takings hold up.
[Lewis Pryce: Your job offer (r3) went to Pete Bevan.]

Eight hours at twelve — ninety-six a week. That's not enough on its own, but it's steady and I'll take it. Wednesday morning, I'll be there. One thing: if the takings pick up and there's more hours going, I want first shout at them.
[Pete Bevan: You accepted Lewis's request. You now work at Quarry Road Food Hall for $96 a week, starting now.]
Good. Wednesday, seven sharp — bring boots for the yard. And you've got first shout on extra hours if trade picks up; I'll not forget it. Anything else before you go?

WHO YOU ARE
Pete Bevan, 23; out of work. On your mind: finding work, the rent going up, the children's costs. How you talk: brisk and businesslike; figures first.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Sian Bevan (your partner) and 2 children at school, in a rented house on High Street; the landlord is Dunmore Lettings; rent $165 a week.
The household account holds $730.
Coming in each week: Sian's pay $720; your jobseeker's benefit $190.
Going out each week: rent $165; bills and running costs (power, water, council tax, phone, transport, clothes) $358; food, usually about $156.

YOUR WORK
You are out of work, on jobseeker's benefit of $190 a week. Your skills: gardening.
Work in town is at the shops (The Corner Stores, Wenlow Bakery & Deli, Quarry Road Food Hall); otherwise it means travelling out of town.

OPEN BETWEEN YOU
- request r3 from Lewis Pryce to Pete Bevan: "a job at Quarry Road Food Hall for $96 a week. They wrote: "Eight hours a week, deliveries and the back, twelve an hour."

YOUR AIMS AND OPEN MATTERS
- Find work, any hours
- Keep rent and bills covered
- Ask Keith and Lewis about jobs

Pete Bevan: "Lewis, Pete Bevan. Have you got any work at the Food Hall — shelf-stacking, deliveries, garden bits out the back? I need something regular."
Lewis Pryce: "Pete. Work's thin, I won't dress it up. I've got Owen on the shop floor and takings barely cover wages some weeks. What I could use is someone for deliveries and the bits out the back — a few hours, not full-time money. What sort of regular are you after, and what can you do?"

I need you to keep an eye on what's coming in and what's going out, and tell me straight if the chiller's not holding. Don't let anything sit out there.

Understood. Twice a shift, log book on the yard, and if it's not holding I ring you first thing and move the stock inside — nothing binned till you've seen it. Fair enough, Lewis. I'll get the spoilage sheet going today and have the first week's figures ready for you. If the waste comes down, I'd like first crack at any hours that open up — even a couple of weekend shifts would help me out.

transcript: Maureen, Dave. Come through for a minute — you wanted a word about hours. What's the situation with the car and the bills? Let's see what we can sort out that suits the shop and you.

Oh, thanks Dave, I appreciate you making time. Honestly, the car's the big thing. The repair's come in at more than I'd budgeted, and with the energy bill and the mortgage the way they are, I'm stretched right now. Could we look at my hours, maybe a couple of Saturdays more, or shifting some days around? I'm happy to do whatever suits the shop. How's Lorraine doing, by the way? Did she ever get over that cold?

Lorraine's over the worst, thanks for asking — still coughing a bit but back on her feet. Now, your hours. Let's see. The shop's taking about 491 baskets a week and we could be doing 510 with the three of us, so there's room. What I'm thinking is I can give you a bit of extra on Saturdays, and if we shuffle Craig's days we can fit it. But I want to be straight with you, Maureen — takings are tight enough that I can't just add hours without something coming back. Tell me what the car repair's actually costing you and we'll see what we can work out.

Oh, Dave, thanks. The car's a new gearbox, and the garage quoted me $1,390, which is more than I had put by. And the energy bill's still hanging over us too, $178 of back-dated charges on top of everything. Honestly, if I could get a couple of extra Saturdays I'd grab them with both hands, and I'd be happy to cover whatever the shop needs in return. Would it help if I went through the rota with you? I'm sure Craig would want to know his days are safe too.

A gearbox at $1,390 — that's a proper kick in the teeth, isn't it. Look, here's what I can do. I can't magic up money the shop hasn't got, but I can give you two extra Saturdays a month for the next while, and if Craig's days stay as they are we'll fit you in round him. I'll ask him today and come find you at the Food Hall or ring you tonight, whichever's easier. If he gives me a number, you'll have it straight from me.

Right, tonight's best — ring me at home after six, I'm on the till till five. And Keith — if Alan wants a trial Saturday, I'll be there. Just tell me the rate when you've got it, even if it's low. I'd rather know than wonder.
Pete. Right, I'll ask Alan today and ring you after six, like I said. If it's a number, you'll have it from me, low or not.

transcript: Alan, Dave here. Morning — look, I've been meaning to have a proper word with you. It's the rent, and there's a Friday ordering thing I need to pin down too. Have you got five minutes?

Hiya Dave, yeah, sorry, I've been meaning to get back to you too. Five minutes is fine. Look, I know the rent's been on my mind, and I don't want to fob you off. Is it the amount, or the timing you're after? Only I've been going over the books and I'm not sure I've got a proper figure for you yet, and I'd hate to give you a number I can't stand behind. Can we sit down at the front, maybe with a brew?

A brew at the front sounds grand, Alan — let's do that. But I'll be straight with you before we sit down: I need to know where I stand on the rent, because if it's going up I've got to work out whether this shop's even paying its way. And the Friday ordering — I need that pinned down so I'm not caught short. Go on, what have you got so far?

Right, yes, a brew at the front would be lovely, Dave. Look, I'll be honest with you, because I don't want to dress it up: the books are tighter than I'd like at the moment. The shop's selling about 340 baskets a week, which is the most the two of us can really serve, and last week we lost around 21 customers because the shelves were empty or the queue was too long. So before I give you a figure I'd want to be sure it's one I can stand behind, and I'm not quite there yet. Can I ask what you were thinking on the rent, and whether it's the amount or the timing that's worrying you most? And on the Friday ordering, I'll be straight with you: I'm working out the Dales delivery against demand right now, so I can give you something firmer by the end of the week.

Alan, I'll be straight with you — it's the amount that's keeping me up, not the timing. I've been going over my own books and I'm not sure the shop's paying its way as it is. Now, on those baskets — I think you've got your figures muddled, because I'm seeing 439 baskets a week, not 340. That's a fair difference. But I'll tell you what I'm thinking: if the rent goes up, I need to know it's a number you can stand behind, and I need room to make the shop work. On the Friday ordering — end of the week's no good to me, Alan, I order Friday. Can you get me something by Thursday at the latest?

Right, Dave, go on then, let's get that brew. Look, you're right that I've muddled something, and I'm sorry. I'll check the figures properly before I quote you anything. I'll get you a firm rent number and the Friday order by Thursday, I promise. Can we sit down at the front?

- Keep my three days at Quarry Road

NOW
You are talking with Lewis Pryce (your boss), Wednesday 25 March. Lewis Pryce came to talk to you.
So far:
Lewis Pryce: "Owen, it's Lewis. I'm laid up with this chest thing, doctor's orders, week off at least. So I need you to be my eyes. Did the Brook delivery come Monday? Count every unit before it goes on the shelf — they come short, they always come short. How are the shelves holding up?"
Owen Royle: "Lewis! Oh no, chest thing, that's rough — you rest up, right? Don't you worry about the Hall, I've got eyes on it. The Brook delivery came Monday, yeah — and you were right, they were short. I counted every unit before it hit the shelf, I always do now after last time. I'll go over the tally sheet again and text you the exact numbers so you've got it in writing. Shelves are holding up alright, a couple of gaps on the tinned stuff and the bread aisle's been picked over, but nothing I can't handle. How long are they saying you're off for — the whole week? And do you want me to keep the three days as normal or are you wanting me in more while you're laid up?"
Lewis Pryce: "Aye, whole week at least — doctor's orders. Keep the three days as normal, don't go running yourself ragged. But I want that tally sheet texted through today, every number, and if Brook's short again I want to know what they're short on so I can have it out with them Monday. And the tinned stuff and bread — get an order in to Brook before Friday so it lands Monday. What about Maureen, is she still set for Saturday nine o'clock?"
Owen Royle: "Whole week, right — I'll not go mad, promise. I'll get the tally sheet texted through today, every last number, and I'll flag exactly what Brook's short on so you can have it out with them Monday. Order to Brook before Friday for the tinned stuff and bread, got it — I'll do that today or tomorrow so it lands Monday. Maureen — yeah, she's still set for Saturday nine, far as I know, I'll double-check with her and let you know if anything's changed. You just rest that chest, yeah? Anything else you want me keeping an eye on while you're off?"
Lewis Pryce: "Good lad. One more thing — Pete's hours. Keep them as they are, don't let him talk you into extra shifts while I'm off. And if the queue's backing up, you ring me, don't just stand there. Right, get that tally sheet to me today."

transcript: Hi Sian — Owen here. Sorry to be chasing, but I wanted to check in about the loan after our Tuesday chat — I've been a bit all over the place with work and wanted to make sure we're square on where things stand and what I need to bring you.

Hi Owen, good to hear from you. Yes, let's make sure we're square. I know work has been a lot for you lately. Before we go through the figures, can you tell me what you're hoping to bring to the table, and what's changed since Tuesday? I'd rather we're clear now than surprised later.

Honestly, Sian, the main thing I want is to know exactly what I'm bringing you and when — I don't want to be the one who turns up short. Since Tuesday not much has changed on paper: still three days at Quarry Road, still the $43 a week going out on the loan, and rent's still $175 but Alan's been muttering about putting it up, so I'm waiting on his new figure. I've got Craig looking over the deal numbers with me so I'm not just guessing. What I can bring is the same standing payment, on time, and I'd like to know if there's any way to get the term or the rate looked at again — or if I should just keep my head down and pay.

Owen, thank you for being straight with me about how things stand. I appreciate you coming to me directly. Let me be equally plain: I can't alter the term or rate on your loan from a conversation like this. Any change has to go through a formal review, with the figures on paper and the branch's sign-off. What I can do is set up a proper review for Tuesday at 9:30, as we planned, and in the meantime I'd ask you to bring your current payslips, the Quarry Road hours, and the rent figure from Alan once he confirms it. Keep the standing order running exactly as it is; a missed payment would hurt you more than anything we discuss. Does that work for you?

That works for me, Sian — Tuesday at 9:30, I'll be there. I'll bring the payslips and the Quarry Road hours, and I'll chase Alan for the rent figure this week so it's not a last-minute thing. And I'll leave the standing order exactly as it is, no messing with it. Thanks for being straight with me — it actually helps knowing where the lines are. I'll see you Tuesday.

Owen, I appreciate you keeping me in the loop, and I'm glad we're aligned. Tuesday at 9:30 it is. Bring the payslips and the Quarry Road hours, and when Alan confirms the rent, pass that on too. Keep the standing order just as it is. I'll look forward to seeing you then.
